newsitem.title: USA: Viacom ends talks with MCA over TV venture.
newsitem.headline: Viacom ends talks with MCA over TV venture.

text.p: Settlement talks between Viacom Inc. and Seagram Co. Ltd. collapsed Friday, setting the stage for the resumption of the companies' courtroom battle for control of their jointly-owned cable network.

The decision, announced just days after the companies had requested an adjournment, came as a surprise because it appeared both sides were close to reaching an agreement that would allow Viacom to acquire Seagram's half of the USA Network in return for Viacom's half of the Sci-Fi channel and a one-time cash payment of around $1.45 billion.
In brief statements, neither company would discuss the reasons for the collapse, but analysts said they would not be surprised if Viacom and Seagram eventually returned to the bargaining table.

"These things have ways of eventually working themselves out but it takes time," said Harold Vogel with Cowen & Co. in New York. "These are stubborn people in a sense so they're holding to their lines of interest."
Proceedings are scheduled to resume on Monday in Delaware Chancery Court with Seagram Chief Executive Edgar Bronfman Jr. testifying.

Viacom, which owns Paramount Pictures, MTV and Nickelodeon, and Seagram, the owner of entertainment and theme park concern MCA Inc., have been fighting for control of the cable channel, with each side accusing the other of violating the terms of their partnership agreement.
The case was put on hold earlier this week to give both sides an opportunity to reach a settlement.

The proposed settlement would have given Viacom sole ownership of the USA cable network, which broadcasts a variety of programmes ranging from re-runs of "Murder, She Wrote" to original movies and the U.S. Open tennis tournament. In return, MCA would have received the less popular Sci-Fi channel, famous for broadcasting re-runs of "Lost in Space" and "The Twilight Zone."

Some analysts said the proposed settlement had appeared to favour Viacom because it gave the New York-based media giant control of the popular cable channel at a time when entertainment companies are scrambling to lock up access for their programmes.

However, Cowen's Vogel said Seagram, which does not own a cable or broadcast network, would also benefit because it would receive enough cash to acquire other interests aimed at expanding MCA's reach into the entertainment industry.
"A billion dollars is a nice piece of change," Vogel said.

Seagram filed suit against Viacom in April, charging the company with violating the terms of the partnership agreement by launching a new cable channel called "Nick at Nite TV Land." Seagram said the partnership prevents either company from operating or launching entertainment cable networks outside of the USA Network.
Viacom contends there was no breach of the partnership, that the partnership was working well and that MCA was trying to get control of USA Network "at an unfairly low price."

USA Network, which reaches 65 million homes, was launched in 1981 by MCA, Paramount Pictures and Time Inc. Time eventually sold out to the partners. In 1994, Paramount was acquired by Viacom and a year later Seagram acquired MCA.

The battle between Viacom and Seagram also puts current MCA Chairman Frank Biondi in a difficult situation because as the former chief executive for Viacom, Biondi had argued the launch of "TV Land" was not a violation of the partnership agreement.
